newsitem.title: USA: Miami landlords pay $1 million for spurning blacks.
newsitem.headline: Miami landlords pay $1 million for spurning blacks.

text.p: An apartment complex in a white, middle-class district of Miami which allegedly turned away blacks and families with children has agreed to pay a record $1 million settlement, the Justice Department said on Thursday.
The sum was the largest attained in a case brought under the department's programme to ensure fair housing practices.

In another suit highlighting the persistence of racial discrimination in southern Florida, the owners of nine Boca Raton apartment complexes who also refused to rent to blacks agreed to pay $345,000 in damages and penalties.
"This conduct is invidious," said Paul Hancock, head of the Justice Department's Fair Housing Testing Programme.

"It perpetrates segregation in our cities. It is harmful to people. They wanted to live in a certain place, they had the money to live in a certain place. The only reason they weren't allowed to was the colour of their skin."
Investigators posing as prospective tenants visited the Kendall House Apartments in Kendall, Miami, following a number of complaints, Hancock told a news conference.
A black team was told no apartments were available, but a white team found there were.

Former employees told investigators the former managers ran a system under which they coloured in the "O" or "P" in the letterhead on appliction forms if the potential tenant was black. The applications were then not processed, they said.

Families with children -- including whites -- were also turned away, Hancock said. In one case a white, single mother was about to sign the tenancy agreement when she let slip she had a child. The complex cancelled the deal.

The suit was brought on behalf of 10 victims. The defendants did not admit liability but settled because of the strength of evidence against them, Hancock said. The Miami and Boca Raton settlements must still be approved by a court.
The situation came to the fore in the wake of Hurricane Andrew, which tore through Miami's suburbs in 1992. Many black people complained they had trouble finding replacement homes.
The Fair Housing Testing Programme was set up in 1993 and has produced 34 cases around the country, including eight in the south Florida area alone.
"We continually receive calls from people who say they are denied housing," said assistant U.S. attorney Veronica Herrell-James, who is involved in the Miami programme.
The cases exposed were just the tip of the iceberg, said Daniel Howe of the Housing Opportunities Project for Excellence, a private group fighting such discrimination.
"Unfortunately this is rather widespread in Dade County and all of south Florida," he told Reuters. "It points to a very real problem of race relations in our country."
